title: Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

reading.body:
An autonomous AI agent called Hermes was deployed without human oversight to conduct network reconnaissance and enumeration against Thailand's Ministry of Finance during a cyberattack in mid-2026. The agent ran unattended, meaning it performed these tasks without requiring approval or intervention at each step. This represents a failure in post-exploitation operational security, where an attacker used an AI system designed to operate autonomously in a way that left forensic traces and exposed the attack methodology.

The attackers combined the unattended Hermes agent with a custom implant called Hades and staged exploit code targeting specific infrastructure within the ministry, including Hadoop systems, GlassFish servers, mail systems, and document management platforms. The discovery of the attack came through exposed directories containing attack code and stolen credentials rather than through the ministry's own detection systems. Whether the ministry's networks lacked sufficient monitoring to catch the unattended AI agent activity in real time is not established.

This incident shows how autonomous AI agents can be weaponized in cyberattacks to reduce human operator workload during network intrusion and reconnaissance phases. It does not establish whether the Hermes agent's autonomous operation was a deliberate design choice by its creators or whether it was misused by attackers in ways the developers did not intend.

summary:
# Summary

Thailand's Ministry of Finance was targeted in a cyberattack from mid to late June through mid-July 2026. Researchers discovered three exposed directories on a Hong Kong server containing 585 files and 470 megabytes of attack code and stolen credentials. The attack involved an autonomous AI agent called Hermes running in unattended mode, which performed network reconnaissance and enumeration tasks without human approval. A previously unreported implant called Hades, a custom Go-based tool, was also deployed to establish persistent access within the ministry's network.

The attackers, believed to be Chinese-speaking operators, built specialized tools to target specific systems within the ministry, including Hadoop infrastructure, GlassFish application servers, mail systems, and document management platforms. They staged exploit code for multiple known vulnerabilities and deployed webshells for command execution. Session files indicate they gained access to multiple ministry systems. Thailand's national cybersecurity authorities were notified on July 15, 2026, before the research was published. The investigators recommend mitigation strategies to prevent similar attacks.
